extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, patent prosecutors, judges, patent examiners, and IP practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and practical rules for construing patent claim terms (how courts determine the meaning and scope of claim language using intrinsic and extrinsic evidence). Applicable to litigation, prosecution, and opinion-drafting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims define the invention/scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The claims define the invention that the patentee is entitled to exclude others from practicing; the written description does not itself delimit the right to exclude — that is the function and purpose of claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with the claims: "The claims define the invention that the patentee is entitled to exclude others from practicing." See Markman. Use claim language as the primary datum for scope determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinary and customary meaning to a person of ordinary skill
rubrics_metrics.description: The words of a claim are generally given their ordinary and customary meaning — the meaning the term would have to a person of ordinary skill in the art as of the effective filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with an objective baseline: how a person of ordinary skill would understand the term. Quote: "the ordinary and customary meaning of a claim term is the meaning the term would have to a person of ordinary skill in the art as of the effective filing date of the patent application."

rubrics_metrics.name: Person of ordinary skill in the art provides context
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim term is to be understood as a skilled artisan would understand it, which provides an objective baseline for interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The skilled artisan is deemed to read the claim term in the context of the particular claim, the entire patent (including specification), and the prosecution history. Use that composite perspective as the starting point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context: consider claim, entire patent, prosecution history
rubrics_metrics.description: Read the disputed term in the context of the particular claim, the entire patent (including the specification), and the prosecution history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context sources include the claim's surrounding words, other claims (both asserted and unasserted), the specification, and the prosecution history. Differences among claims (claim differentiation) are a useful guide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intrinsic evidence is primary
rubrics_metrics.description: Intrinsic evidence — the claims, specification, and prosecution history — is the most important source for claim construction; the specification is usually dispositive and is the single best guide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "The specification is always highly relevant and usually is dispositive; it is the single best guide to the meaning of a disputed term." Courts should rely heavily on the written description for guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification governs special definitions and disclaimers
rubrics_metrics.description: A special definition in the specification for a claim term (including implied definitions) will govern; an intentional disclaimer or disavowal in the specification is dispositive of claim scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentees acting as their own lexicographers can define terms; if the specification reveals clear disavowal, that limits claim scope. Look for explicit definitions or language of manifest exclusion or restriction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution history (file history) is relevant but less useful than specification
rubrics_metrics.description: The prosecution history can show how the inventor understood the invention and whether the inventor limited the invention during prosecution, but it often lacks the clarity of the specification and is thus less useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use prosecution history to exclude interpretations disclaimed during prosecution. Treat it as an ongoing negotiation with the PTO — informative but not definitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extrinsic evidence is subordinate to intrinsic evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Extrinsic evidence (e.g., dictionaries, learned treatises, expert testimony) may be used to assist the court but is generally less significant than the intrinsic record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extrinsic evidence may educate the court about the field or meaning of terms but should be considered only in the context of intrinsic evidence and given appropriate weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dictionaries can be useful but have limits
rubrics_metrics.description: General-purpose and technical dictionaries may be consulted to understand commonly understood words or technical usages, especially in simple cases, but they cannot override definitions found in the patent documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dictionaries are unbiased, publicly accessible resources and may help judges in simple cases; however, a dictionary's abstract meaning may miss context — the ordinary meaning is what the skilled artisan would derive after reading the entire patent. Avoid "dictionaries first" approach that leads to systematic overbreadth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert testimony can assist but must be reliable
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert testimony can explain background technology, how an invention works, and how a person of skill would understand a term, but conclusory or unsupported expert assertions are not useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts should provide objective, supportable explanations; courts should discount testimony clearly at odds with the written record or that is biased/litigation-directed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extrinsic evidence reliability concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Extrinsic evidence may be unreliable because it was not created during prosecution, may not reflect skilled artisans' understanding, may be biased for litigation, and experts may lack relevant skill or be presented without cross-examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess extrinsic materials critically: consider contemporaneity, intended audience, potential bias, and whether the expert is truly skilled in the relevant art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court has discretion to admit and weigh extrinsic evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: District courts may, in their sound discretion, admit and use extrinsic evidence to educate themselves regarding the field and to determine what a person of ordinary skill would understand, but must keep in mind intrinsic evidence's primacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use extrinsic evidence to supplement the intrinsic record only when helpful and evaluate its credibility and consistency with the patent documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence of evidence consultation is flexible
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no required sequence for consulting sources (claims, specification, prosecution history, dictionaries, experts); courts are not barred from consulting any particular source or required to analyze sources in a specific order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A judge might start with a dictionary or technical treatise to get background, then read the patent to determine how the patentee used the term. More important is the weight attached to sources, not order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function (§112, para. 6) rule application
rubrics_metrics.description: Means-plus-function rules apply only to purely functional claim limitations that do not recite the structure performing the recited function; if the claim recites structure, the means-plus-function rule does not apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim recites physical structure (e.g., "baffles") rather than a bare functional recital, treat it as structural and construe its proper meaning rather than invoking §112(6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim differentiation as a guide
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences among claims (particularly dependent claims that add limitations) can be valuable in understanding whether a limitation is inherent in an independent claim; the presence of a dependent claim adding a limitation raises a presumption that the independent claim lacks that limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine dependent claims: if a dependent claim explicitly adds a feature, it is evidence that the independent claim did not already contain that feature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must enable all claims but embodiments do not necessarily limit every claim
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must teach and enable all the claims, but descriptions of particular embodiments or objectives (e.g., deflecting projectiles) do not automatically restrict all claims to those objectives unless the claim language or specification clearly requires it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specification to enable claim scope; do not import limitations from preferred embodiments into claim scope absent clear intent to limit. Example: description of baffles deflecting projectiles enables dependent claims that claim that function but does not limit all claims to that function.

rubrics_metrics.name: A claim need not achieve every objective stated in the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact the patent asserts several objectives does not require each claim be construed as limited to structures capable of achieving all those objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between embodiments/advertised advantages and the actual claim language; do not construe independent claims to require capabilities only recited in some embodiments or dependent claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construing to preserve validity is limited
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have recognized that claims may be construed to preserve validity, but that maxim is applied narrowly — only when, after applying all available claim construction tools, the claim remains ambiguous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not make validity-preserving constructions routine; apply only as a last resort when ambiguity persists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction should "stay true" to claim language and align with specification
rubrics_metrics.description: The correct construction is the one that stays true to the claim language and most naturally aligns with the patent's description of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for the construction that best matches the ordinary meaning to the skilled artisan while being consistent with the patent's specification and prosecution history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjective inventor testimony is of limited weight
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjective inventor testimony about what was intended to be claimed is heavily discounted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on objective intrinsic evidence and credible extrinsic support about the skilled artisan's understanding rather than on inventor's post hoc assertions of intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide evidence to establish key factual predicates
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence establishing who is a person of ordinary skill and how that person would understand claim terms is central to claim construction, but must be consistent with the patent document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asserting a particular construction, supply contemporaneous technical definitions, treatises, or credible expert analysis tied to the intrinsic record to show how a skilled artisan would read the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts should weigh sources appropriately; no single source is dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: While intrinsic evidence is generally most valuable, courts must attach appropriate weight to all available sources and avoid rigid algorithms that improperly elevate dictionaries or other extrinsic materials over the patent documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Vitronics/Markman principles: intrinsic evidence > extrinsic evidence for meanings, but use commonsense balancing and avoid mechanical checklisting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal Circuit review and standard of law
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim construction is treated as a legal question subject to plenary review by the Federal Circuit (per en banc Phillips), though some judges dissent that factual aspects may warrant deference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate that claim constructions may be reviewed de novo at the appellate level; ensure the record explains interpretive choices and factual predicates clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case-specific extraction of requirements from claim language
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts should extract explicit requirements from the claim language itself (e.g., in the Phillips case the claim language imposed three clear requirements on 'baffles': made of steel; part of load-bearing means; pointed inward from the walls).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When construing a term, list explicit limitations present in the claim text rather than importing unclaimed features from embodiments; use the claim wording to identify discrete requirements.
